stories.title: Spain: A Small Provincial City Leads the Country
paragraphs: Spain's largest source of campers isn't Madrid or Barcelona but Cáceres, a city of about 100,000 people in Extremadura. Cáceres has sent 28 campers since 2005, more than Madrid and Barcelona combined. Extremadura as a whole supplies 53% of Spain's campers, against 2% of the population.

The Cáceres pipeline is unusually steady. It has sent a camper in every year from 2005 to 2023 except 2012, and it is still active. Its campers turned Spain from an occasional sender (eight campers before 2000) into one of Europe's larger ones.

Spain had one earlier, shorter cluster: eight campers from the Basque Country, mostly Vitoria-Gasteiz, in 2003–2008. Andalusia, Catalonia and Valencia, home to almost half of Spaniards, have sent five campers between them.

Because few people move to Cáceres after camp, this cluster almost certainly reflects where campers lived when they attended. It most likely traces back to a local school, teacher or alumnus who has been selecting campers there for nearly two decades.

stories.title: Greece: From Athens to Thessaloniki
paragraphs: Greece shows the clearest shift in location of any country in the directory. Before 2000, 75% of Greek campers came from Athens and the surrounding Attica region. From 2000 on, only 5% did. Over the same years, Central Macedonia, mostly Thessaloniki and its suburbs, went from 18% of Greek campers to 84%.

Athens campers span 1955–2005, with a median year of 1980. Thessaloniki's first camper attended in 1983, and the city has sent campers almost every year since 2002. Central Macedonia now supplies 60% of all Greek campers, against 17% of the population.
A change this sharp suggests that the alumni network selecting Greece's campers moved its base from Athens to Thessaloniki around 2000.

stories.title: Ireland: Most Campers Are From Northern Ireland
paragraphs: The directory lists 26 campers under Ireland, but only eight have an address in the Republic. The other 18 list Enniskillen or County Fermanagh, in Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom.
All 18 Fermanagh campers attended between 1998 and 2005, starting the year of the Good Friday Agreement.
Without them, the Republic of Ireland has sent eight campers: four from Limerick (2001–2005), two from Dublin and one each from Kildare and Kerry. No new Irish camper is listed after 2005.

stories.title: Germany: A Rhineland Network
paragraphs: North Rhine-Westphalia supplies 47 of Germany's 84 placed campers (56%), against 22% of the population. Unlike most clusters in this directory, these campers don't come from a single city. They are spread across Cologne, Bonn, Wuppertal, Erkrath, Solingen, Essen and other nearby towns.
The region has also sent campers steadily since 1968, with at least one in most years since 2000. Both features point to a regional alumni network rather than a single school or contact.
Berlin is the other over-represented region, with 15 campers (seven of them in 2005–2008). Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, home to almost a third of Germans, have sent seven campers between them.

stories.title: Who Recruits Nationally, and Who Recruits From the Capital
paragraphs: The Netherlands, Denmark and Poland are the most evenly spread senders in the whole directory. Each has over 80 campers, and each draws them from nearly every region in close to population proportions. Poland has campers from 15 of its 16 provinces, and the Netherlands from all 12 of its.

Most other large European senders draw mainly from the capital. Paris and its region supply 85% of France's campers, and Rome 85% of Italy's. Greater Stockholm supplies 80% of Sweden's campers, while Gothenburg's region, home to about a sixth of Swedes, has sent none. Since each country's campers are selected by a local alumni network, this largely reflects where that network's members live and work.

stories.title: Small-Town Clusters
paragraphs: Several countries have a burst of campers from one smaller town or district, usually over just a few years. Clusters in small places are among the most reliable findings in the directory, since few people move to them after camp. Each probably reflects one well-placed contact in the local alumni network.

Montreuil, an eastern suburb of Paris, sent nine campers in 2013–2020. In Russia, Volgograd and neighboring Volzhsky sent five campers in 1990–1993, before Russia's campers shifted to Moscow and St Petersburg. Finland's Lapland region, mostly Rovaniemi, sent seven campers in 2004–2014.

stories.title: Northern Roots: Small Countries, Many Campers
paragraphs: Europe has supplied over half of all CRS campers in every period of camp history, between 51% and 62%.

CRS's founding era was Northern European. Before 1970, the UK, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and the Netherlands supplied 90 of Europe's 125 campers. These countries have kept sending campers ever since. The Netherlands has had a camper in almost every year since 1970, and Denmark and Finland have never gone more than five years without one.

The result is that Europe's smallest established senders are its largest relative to population. Denmark, with six million people, has sent more campers than Germany, with 84 million. Finland and Norway, with under six million each, have each sent more than France or Italy.

stories.title: Eastern Europe: Campers Through the Cold War and After
paragraphs: Eastern European countries sent campers even during the Cold War. Poland had 15 campers under communism, the first in 1957. Hungary sent one camper a year in 1986–1989. Yugoslavia sent four campers in 1970–1975, Czechoslovakia two (1968 and 1975) and Romania one (1975).

After 1989, campers came from countries that had just opened up or come out of conflict. All 13 of Russia's campers attended in 1990–1999. Bosnia and Herzegovina sent three campers in 1996–1997, just after the war. Poland and Hungary grew into two of Europe's largest senders, and together supplied 16 of Europe's 59 campers since 2020.
Several of Eastern Europe's largest countries are still barely represented. Russia, with 144 million people, has had no camper since 1999. Ukraine has sent four campers and Romania one, in 1975.

stories.title: The 2001–2010 Wave
paragraphs: Between 2001 and 2010, 13 European countries sent 73 campers. None of these countries had a camper before 2001, and none has had a new camper since 2010. Six of them (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Malta) joined the European Union in 2004. The others are Portugal, Iceland, Luxembourg, Austria, Belarus, Albania and Moldova.

These countries sent six to 11 campers a year in 2001–2009, then one in 2010. They account for most of the jump from 22 European countries sending campers in the 1990s to 33 in the 2000s, and for the fall back to 18 in the 2010s.

The timing points to a dedicated programme or funding stream that ended around 2009–2010, when camp-wide listings also halved. It would be worth asking CRS what it was. These 13 countries are places where CRS once had working connections, which may make them good starting points for renewed recruitment.

stories.title: Western Europe's Recent Decline
paragraphs: Since 2010, Europe's campers have come from fewer countries, and the mix has shifted away from some of the largest Western European senders.

The UK fell from 32 campers in the 2000s to 17 in the 2010s and three since 2020. France's last listed camper attended in 2020, at the end of the Montreuil cluster, and Italy's in 2019. Recent years are undercounted in the directory, because new alumni take time to register. But Poland, Denmark, Germany, Hungary and Spain together have 37 campers listed since 2020, so the drop for the UK, France and Italy stands out.
